analysis.one_liner: Gives consumers a free yearly credit report and the right to see their credit score.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 10 cosponsors, the bill was referred to a House Financial Services subcommittee on April 10, 2001, and never received a hearing or vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act so any consumer could get one free credit report each year on request, and could see the credit scores and risk predictions in their file, including the factors used and how much each factor raises or lowers the score. It would also keep small old debts (under $100 and more than 3 years old) off a credit report in some cases, and direct the Federal Reserve and FTC to monitor whether credit bureaus actually investigate and fix disputed errors.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a credit file — essentially every adult who has used a credit card, taken out a loan, or financed a purchase. Under the law at the time, consumers could be charged to see their own credit report, and credit scores were explicitly exempt from disclosure, so people denied credit often had no way to learn their score or why it was low. The bill would give every consumer one free report a year, full access to their scores with an explanation of the factors and weights behind them, online contact information for the bureaus, and a path to having small old debts wiped from their report after completing a credit education class.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each consumer reporting agency to provide a free credit report to any consumer who requests one, once every calendar year.

Ends the exemption that kept credit scores and other risk scores secret: agencies would have to disclose all scores in the consumer's file, with a summary of how they are derived, the factors used, the relative weight of each factor, and how the factors raise or lower the score.
Requires agencies to give consumers information sufficient to contact them or request a report through the Internet or World Wide Web.

Excludes from credit reports collection accounts or charge-offs of $100 or less that are more than 3 years old, if the consumer completed a credit and financial management class in that period and has not used this exclusion before.

Directs the Federal Reserve Board and the FTC to review and monitor whether credit bureaus and the companies that supply them data are promptly investigating disputes and correcting or deleting inaccurate, incomplete, or unverifiable information, and to report to Congress with recommendations within 6 months of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer reporting agencies (the credit bureaus) and credit score developers, whose core consumer-facing business is selling people their own reports and scores. A free annual report and mandatory score disclosure would cut directly into that revenue, and the dispute-monitoring provisions would put furnisher and bureau error-correction practices under federal scrutiny.

drawbacks.text: The dispute-error provisions are study-only: the bill directs the Federal Reserve and FTC to monitor compliance and report with recommendations, but imposes no new enforcement, penalties, or rules on its own.
The small-debt relief is narrow — it applies only to accounts of $100 or less that are more than 3 years old, only after the consumer completes a credit class, and only once per consumer.
The free report is available only on request, so its value depends on consumers knowing to ask; the bill creates no automatic delivery or reminder system.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that giving every requesting consumer a free report each year shifts real fulfillment costs onto the bureaus, which could seek to recover them elsewhere in their business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main consumer gains — a free annual credit report and the right to see your own credit score with an explanation — are real and directly address a situation where people were charged to see their own data and denied the score that decided their credit. The weaknesses are that the error-correction section is only a study, and the small-debt exclusion is so narrow it helps few people. On balance a modest, well-aimed consumer bill whose costs fall on a small industry rather than on the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and sat there without any action until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Harold Ford Jr. introduced the bill on March 22, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
On April 10, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit — the last action the bill ever received.
The bill attracted 10 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no further action, hearings, markup, or floor vote is recorded before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The credit bureaus and credit score developers. Nothing changed, so they kept charging consumers for their own reports, kept scores exempt from disclosure, and faced no new scrutiny of how they handle disputed errors.

for.name: Rep. Harold Ford Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 22, 2001, to require free annual credit reports, disclosure of credit scores, and federal monitoring of dispute-resolution practices.

for.name: 10 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the record shows no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee and its Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee on April 10, 2001, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Consumer reporting agencies (credit bureaus) and credit score developers
against.what_they_did: Credit bureaus and score vendors such as the major national bureaus had long operated on charging consumers for their own reports and keeping credit scores exempt from disclosure, and the industry opposed mandates to disclose scores and their underlying factors.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill died in a committee then controlled by the Republican majority without ever reaching the floor; no roll-call votes were ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would require a free credit report every year on request and web contact information, cutting into the bureaus' consumer-paid report revenue, and would put their dispute and error-correction practices under Fed and FTC review. Their interest in keeping reports paid and scores hidden runs directly against consumers' ability to check and challenge their own files.

Federal law at the time explicitly exempted credit scores from consumer disclosure; the bill would force disclosure of scores along with the factors, their relative weights, and how they raise or lower the score. Score vendors relied on that secrecy, since consumers unable to see their scores could not question them.

industries.industry: Furnishers of consumer data to credit bureaus (lenders, collectors)
industries.note: The bill directs regulators to monitor whether these companies promptly comply with duties to investigate disputes and correct or delete unverifiable information, and the small-debt provision would keep some old small collection accounts off reports. Companies whose sloppy reporting drives credit errors would face scrutiny of practices that cost consumers loans and higher rates.
